body.text: In short:

Former military lawyer David McBride says senior Australian Defence Force commanders have not faced the level of scrutiny soldiers have over the culture within Australia's SAS during the war in Afghanistan.
The whistleblower is currently on parole after serving more than two years behind bars for leaking secret military documents to journalists.
What's next?
McBride will be honoured by a group of former intelligence officers with the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence on Tuesday.
After more than two years in prison, former military lawyer turned whistleblower David McBride says he is finally "coming back to the surface".
"You don't get out of jail the day you leave. You do get out of jail once your brain starts to relax a little."
In his first sit-down interview since leaving jail on parole in August, David McBride told Radio National Breakfast about the toll time in prison took on him.
"It's not easy. It was pretty hard in prison, and it's pretty hard when you get out.
"There's a certain amount of, 'You never want to let your enemy see you bleed,'" says McBride. "But yeah, it takes its toll."
McBride was sentenced to five years and eight months jail in 2024, after pleading guilty to three charges relating to sharing secret documents with journalists.

The former military lawyer has previously said he gave secret defence material to an ABC journalist for the purpose of exposing what he thought was the "over-investigation" of special forces soldiers in Afghanistan.
But the material he provided did the opposite.
The seven-part series his information produced, known as The Afghan Files, revealed the alleged involvement of Australian soldiers in unlawful killings.
Calls for ADF leadership to face scrutiny
McBride maintains he was a whistleblower against the leadership of the Australian Defence Force, and believes they are yet to face adequate scrutiny over allegations of war crimes in Afghanistan.
"The soldiers at the coalface, they have been raked over the coals," says McBride. "The command have not had anything like that scrutiny. And it is absolutely a command-led structure."
Stronger scrutiny of those in defence command structures is essential to the ADF's future, McBride says.
"As I've always said, it's not about the last war, it's about the next war."

McBride welcomed the recent publication of a long-secret inquiry into the cultural and command failures of Australian special forces operators during the war in Afghanistan which found an "abandonment of curiosity" within the ADF's leadership and an "inversion of authority" within units helped create a culture that allowed alleged war crimes to occur.
"I think that that is, that's accurate, and good on the Defence Force for actually allowing that introspective.
"That's the sort of thing that I wanted all along. Some sort of admission that, yes, in a war, the truth is going to get massaged, but there are limits," says McBride.
"And if I've just made the ADF be a little bit more introspective about how far they can push those boundaries, I will have achieved something."
The chief of the ADF, Admiral Mark Hammond, later told Senate estimates that "all departmental actions relevant to that inquiry have been completed."
McBride's actions recognised by intelligence community

The Sam Adams Associates for Integrity in Intelligence have announced McBride as the 2026 winner of its award, which was set up in 2002 in memory of the late CIA analyst Sam Adams and is presented each year to a member of the intelligence, military or national security community.

"As a whistleblower, you often feel that people look at you and say, 'Oh, well, he just couldn't handle it. He was someone that didn't really understand, you know, it's 'big boys' games, big boys' rules,'" says McBride.
But the former military lawyer says being recognised by fellow "hard-nosed" intelligence analysts means a lot to him.

"It means that people who get it, people who have seen secrets, people who believe in their countries, have said, 'Yeah, you are one of us'. That probably means more to me than any other kind of recognition."
'I'd absolutely do it again'
McBride is currently serving the remaining three years of his sentence in the community under supervision and conditions.
He says that despite some criticism of his actions, he is proud of what he did.
"I'd absolutely do it again," McBride says, "I like the person I am. My kids like the person I am, and that's important to me. And you can only really ask for that.
"I've always wanted to do something positive for the country. I believe I've done that."
McBride says he is planning to spend his new-found freedom writing.
He is currently working on a book about why he decided to leak the secret defence documents, and is planning a second book about his time in prison.
"It's a life I've always wanted, a big life. But yeah, it comes at a cost. There's no doubt about it."
Additional reporting by Oscar Coleman and Kimberley Price
